lines.text: Walls lower the risk. They don't remove it. Here is what remains.
Bugs. KVM and Firecracker are code too, and flaws are found in them now and then.

lines.text: The answer is boring, and it works: keep the host's kernel and Firecracker up to date.
The processor itself. In 2018, attacks like Spectre showed that a program can guess secrets from how fast the processor answers.
Kernel and processor updates block the known ones. The host must have them.
The biggest risk is in the box. It reaches the internet.
Any secret you put in it, a token, a password, can be sent away by the code you run, or by an agent tricked into doing it.
A box can also be turned against others: mining, spam, attacks.
That is why its bandwidth is capped, and outgoing mail on port twenty-five is blocked.
So a sandbox doesn't make code trustworthy. It decides how far the damage can go.
Give each box only what it needs, and keep the walls up to date.
